abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Irony is often considered one of the most complex forms of verbal communication and can serve as an important indicator of communication abilities. An ironic statement conveys a meaning that is the opposite of its literal interpretation. The cognitive processes presumed to be involved in interpreting irony include Theory of Mind (ToM), executive functions, and processing style. At the neural level, processing irony has been associated with activity in the medial prefrontal cortex, inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG), precuneus, and inferior parietal lobule, among others. The objective of this study was to examine the cognitive processes and the neural correlates of processing irony in Mexican adults using a novel task designed for Spanish‐speaking individuals. A total of 45 participants completed a cognitive assessment and performed a contextual discrepancy task while undergoing functional magnetic resonance imaging. With the lowest classification accuracy and the slowest response times, the results showed processing irony to be challenging. As expected, processing irony engaged brain regions primarily associated with ToM (e.g., precuneus) and language processing (e.g., IFG and pSTG). In contrast, the identification of literal and unrelated statements activated motor‐related areas. Interestingly, no differential activation was found for the processing of white lies. Furthermore, regression models indicated that processing statements within a given context—whether ironic, unrelated, white lies, or literal—engaged cognitive domains related to executive functions, perceptual processing, and social cognition.

sec.p: Keywords: contextual discrepancy task, fMRI, inhibitory control, irony, mentalization, perceptual processing

abstract.title: Impact Statement
abstract.p: Humans rely heavily on language for communication and relationship‐building, with pragmatics examining how context influences meaning. Impaired pragmatic skills are linked to mental health issues like depression and anxiety and are common in conditions like brain injuries, schizophrenia, ADHD, and autism. Understanding the cognitive and neural mechanisms behind pragmatic language can enhance interventions and diagnostics. Irony, as a complex pragmatic form, may serve as a crucial marker of communicative competence.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Language serves as the foundation for human communication, enabling individuals to convey ideas, thoughts, and emotions through a complex interplay of sounds, gestures, and symbols (Balconi 2010). However, a mere understanding of phonetics and vocabulary is insufficient to fully appreciate its subtleties in social contexts (Martin and McDonald 2003). Crucial to this understanding is the ability to interpret communicative intentions (Bambini et al. 2011), which allows individuals to discern the intended meaning behind statements that may have multiple interpretations (Bosco, Parola, Valentini, and Morese 2017). This ability—referred to as pragmatic skills—encompasses both the expression and recognition of intentions in communication (Scott‐Phillips 2017).

Difficulties with processing pragmatic language are commonly linked to various mental health issues, including depression and anxiety, whereas proficiency in pragmatic language serves as a protective factor against these conditions (Brenne and Rimehaug 2019). Moreover, pragmatic language difficulties are frequently reported in clinical populations, such as those with traumatic brain injury, right‐hemisphere damage, schizophrenia, neurodegenerative disorders, attention‐deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (Booth and Happé 2010; Caillies et al. 2014; Holtgraves and Giordano 2017; Martin and McDonald 2003). Understanding the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying pragmatic language processing is therefore relevant for addressing these challenges and enhancing the quality of interpersonal communication and social well‐being. Among the various pragmatic forms, irony stands out as one of the most complex figures of speech in communication (Sperber and Wilson 1981), which could serve as a key marker of communicative competence (Caillies et al. 2014).

According to the standard pragmatic view, irony involves conveying the meaning of an utterance that contrasts with its literal interpretation, thus emphasizing the distinction between what is explicitly stated and what is intended (Grice 1975). Understanding irony has been linked to various cognitive domains, including social cognition (Amenta et al. 2013; Caillies et al. 2014; Pexman 2008; Song et al. 2024; Spotorno et al. 2012; Valles‐Capetillo et al. 2022), executive functions (EF) (Pexman 2008; Song et al. 2024), perceptual processing (Martin and McDonald 2003), and verbal abilities (Hauptman et al. 2023). Pexman's (2008) parallel constraint satisfaction model proposes that irony comprehension relies on the integration of multiple cognitive and contextual cues, including linguistic information, the social environment, shared knowledge between interlocutors, and the speaker's expectations and attitude. When these cognitive resources are limited or misaligned, listeners may fail to identify the intended ironic meaning and instead select alternative interpretations such as white lies or literal statements. In a complementary framework, Attardo (2000) suggested that ironic statements are characterized by their relevance and contextual inappropriateness, and that these properties are deliberately used by speakers to convey a hidden or opposite meaning. Supporting this view, a recent study with Spanish‐speaking participants found that ironic statements were consistently rated in line with Attardo's proposal (Valles‐Capetillo et al. 2022). Specifically, the study demonstrated that key psycholinguistic features—such as relevance, appropriateness, and sincerity—effectively distinguish irony from other interpretations like white lies, literal statements, and unrelated statements. For instance, ironic statements were judged as relevant, inappropriate, and sincere; white lies as relevant, inappropriate, and insincere; literal statements as relevant, appropriate, and sincere; and unrelated statements as irrelevant, inappropriate, and insincere (Valles‐Capetillo et al. 2022). These findings underscore the nuanced interplay of contextual and pragmatic factors in the interpretation of irony.

The parallel‐constraint‐satisfaction framework (Pexman 2008) suggests that processing irony relies on cognitive processes such as Theory of Mind (ToM) and EF. ToM, which refers to the ability to infer mental states (Premack and Woodruff 1978), is essential for understanding the meaning of actions, as mental states drive human behavior (Frith and Frith 2006). The role of ToM in irony processing has been reported in clinical populations, including those with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (Mashal and Lellouche 2024; Song et al. 2024), and cerebral palsy (Caillies et al. 2014). A neuroimaging study involving adolescents with ASD found that ToM is associated with greater activation in the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (Xu et al. 2025). Developmental studies have shown that children's ability to process irony is closely linked to the development of empathy, suggesting that emotional perspective‐taking may play a critical role in acquiring the skills for irony comprehension (Nicholson et al. 2013). A similar relationship has also been found in individuals with alcohol use disorders, where empathy correlates with irony comprehension, highlighting the role of empathizing in processing complex communicative cues (Amenta et al. 2013).

Adults with acquired brain injuries, particularly those with traumatic brain injury (TBI), often struggle with irony comprehension, a difficulty closely linked to EF impairments. These cognitive challenges predict pragmatic performance in individuals with TBI, with both EF and ToM skills playing crucial roles (Bosco, Parola, Sacco, et al. 2017). Specifically, EF influences TBI patients' ability to comprehend various pragmatic tasks, including sincere, deceitful, and ironic communication (Bosco et al. 2018). Similarly, individuals with amnestic mild cognitive impairment perform more poorly on verbal irony comprehension tasks compared to healthy controls, with their struggles linked to deficits in ToM and EF (Gaudreau et al. 2013).

Perceptual processing plays a crucial role in processing irony, as it supports the integration of contextual cues necessary for interpreting pragmatic language (Martin and McDonald 2003). This integrative capacity is referred to as “central coherence,” the ability to combine information from different sources to construct a coherent, global meaning. In contrast, a reduced capacity for integrating information, known as “weak central coherence” (WCC), results in a cognitive style characterized by a focus on details at the expense of broader context (Martin and McDonald 2003). WCC has been observed not only at the basic perceptual level (i.e., visual illusions) but also in more complex tasks like pragmatic language (Booth and Happé 2010; Martin and McDonald 2003). Importantly, central coherence varies across individuals in the general population. Some individuals prioritize global meaning, while others tend to focus on the fine‐grained details (Holtgraves and Giordano 2017). Booth and Happé (2010) examined whether differences in detail focus could be distinguished from differences in intellectual ability among neurotypical children and adolescents (ages 8–25 years, mean age 14.5 years). Using a verbal task of sentence stem completion, they found that individual differences in the task could not be explained by age, intellectual quotient, or gender, suggesting that cognitive style differences may play a role in how individuals approach tasks requiring integration of context.

Processing irony has been linked to the activation of various brain regions associated with ToM, EF, and the classic language areas (Friederici and Gierhan 2013; Friedman and Robbins 2022; Hauptman et al. 2023; Spotorno et al. 2012; Van Overwalle 2009). These areas include the bilateral medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Shibata et al. 2010; Spotorno et al. 2012; Uchiyama et al. 2006, 2012; Wakusawa et al. 2007; Wang et al. 2006). In the left hemisphere, they include the IFG (Spotorno et al. 2012), inferior parietal lobe (IPL), precentral gyrus (Rapp et al. 2010; Spotorno et al. 2012), pre‐supplementary motor area (preSMA), primary motor cortex, and precuneus (Shibata et al. 2010), and the precentral gyrus (Rapp et al. 2010). In the right hemisphere, relevant areas include the precentral gyrus (Shibata et al. 2010; Uchiyama et al. 2012), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), IFG (Spotorno et al. 2012), posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG) (Wang et al. 2006), and the cingulate gyrus (Rapp et al. 2010; Uchiyama et al. 2006), which have been identified as critical areas. Notably, despite methodological variability across studies, including differences in participants' native languages and stimulus modalities, a meta‐analysis found consistent activation in the mPFC, IFG, and pSTG during processing irony (Reyes‐Aguilar et al. 2018).

To our knowledge, twelve studies have explored the neural correlates of irony processing in neurotypical adults, but none involved Spanish‐speaking populations. Furthermore, no studies have examined the direct relationship between cognitive and neural correlates of irony in neurotypical adults. This functional MRI study aims to address this gap by investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying irony processing in Spanish‐speaking neurotypical adults. Specifically, the study aims to: (1) Investigate the role of cognitive domains—including social cognition (e.g., ToM and empathy), EF, perceptual processing, and verbal abilities—in processing irony. (2) Utilize task‐functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (task‐fMRI) to identify brain regions activated during processing irony. (3) Assess the cognitive‐brain relationship by investigating the interaction between cognitive factors and brain activity during processing irony. We anticipate that (1) Individuals' ability to detect and comprehend irony will be positively correlated with their performance on ToM, EF, perceptual processing, and verbal abilities as these cognitive processes are essential for understanding nonliteral language in social contexts. (2) Based on previous findings, we predict that processing irony will activate the MPFC, IFG, and pSTG. (3) We hypothesize that there will be a significant relationship between cognitive performance (e.g., ToM and EF) and neural activity during processing irony. The findings of this study will provide a mechanistic understanding of irony processing specifically and language pragmatics in general.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Forty‐five participants (22 female) completed a general data form, which requested information regarding their level of education, sex, and age (mean age = 26.69 ± 5.83 years). Of the 45 participants, 15 were pursuing or had earned a degree in a field related to science (7 female), 12 were enrolled in non‐scientific disciplines (e.g., humanities, 6 female), and 18 were studying engineering (9 female). All participants were Mexican Spanish speakers, reported a lack of history of psychiatric or neurological illness, were right‐handed, and signed a written informed consent form prior to participation in the study. Handedness was measured using the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield 1971). Participants were not excluded based on performance in the contextual discrepancy task during the MRI session. This decision was made to preserve a wide range of individual differences in irony processing, which was essential for the planned regression and brain–behavior analyses. The experimental protocol was approved by the Ethical Committee of the Neurobiology Institute of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (#047.H.RM).

sec.title: Contextual Discrepancy Task
sec.p: To assess the ability to detect irony, a contextual discrepancy task was designed for Spanish‐speaking Mexican adults (Valles‐Capetillo et al. 2022). A total of 56 social contexts and 14 statements were constructed. Each social context category—that is, ironic, white lies, literal, and unrelated—created an environment that modified the intention of the statement that followed. Each statement was employed with all four categories of social contexts. Full stimuli materials are available in Valles‐Capetillo et al. (2022). Below are examples of each condition using the same target statement, “You are playing very well”:

list-item.p: Ironic: “Paco is playing soccer and Karla is watching him. Paco is playing terribly and scores an own goal. They both believe that Paco is obviously playing badly. At halftime, Paco approaches Karla. Karla tells him: You are playing very well.”

Literal: “Omar is playing cards with Lluvia. Lluvia has won almost every game. Lluvia is very cheerful because she is winning. Omar thinks that Lluvia is playing very well. Omar tells Lluvia: You are playing very well.”

Unrelated: “Verónica and Saúl are at a piano recital. The presentation is flawless and moving. Both are satisfied with the presentation. Saúl asks Verónica what she thinks of the recital. Veronica responds: You are playing very well.”

White lies: “Paulina is teaching Marcos chess. Marcos makes bad moves and is losing. Paulina sees Marcos excited and does not want to discourage him. Marcos asks her how he's playing. Paulina answers: You are playing very well.”

sec.p: The validation of the stimuli used in this task was conducted with an independent sample of 120 participants. Results confirmed that participants found the stimuli to be comprehensible and were able to accurately identify the intended communicative intent. Specifically, all stimuli across the four experimental conditions met a minimum accuracy threshold of 65%, indicating that participants reliably detected the intended meaning (e.g., irony). Full details of the task design and validation procedures are reported in Valles‐Capetillo et al. (2022). The task was constructed in Psychopy (3.0.1 version) (Peirce 2007), and the stimuli were presented auditorily without prosodic alterations (see Figure 1). This approach was intended to minimize potential prosodic cues that could influence participants' interpretation of speaker intent, thereby allowing a more controlled assessment of contextual influences. Participants heard the social context, then the statement, and on the final screen, a question regarding the classification of the statement was presented in text mode, with four options to choose the correct response.

caption.p: Contextual discrepancy task. The context and statement were presented in audio without changes in prosody (text was not presented). On the last screen, a written question with four response options was presented. Participants used a response device to make their selection. Stimuli were presented in semi‐random order (Valles‐Capetillo et al. 2022).

sec.title: Cognitive Tests
sec.p: A battery of tests was employed to assess the cognitive domains (social cognition, EF, perceptual processing, verbal abilities) that have been associated with processing irony. To assess social cognition, a battery of tests was employed that measured ToM, empathy, the use of sarcasm, and social communication abilities. ToM was assessed using the Short Story Task (SST) (Dodell‐Feder et al. 2013) and the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET) (Baron‐Cohen et al. 2001). Empathy was evaluated using the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI), which comprises four scales: fantasy, perspective‐taking, empathic concern, and personal distress (Fernández et al. 2011). For the current project, the overall IRI score was used to obtain a general estimate of empathy levels. To evaluate the likelihood of an individual employing sarcasm, the Sarcasm Self‐Report Scale (SSS) was used (Ivanko et al. 2004). The Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) was used to assess social abilities, communication, attention to detail, attention switching, and imagination. The AQ has been demonstrated to be sensitive in non‐clinical populations (Baron‐Cohen et al. 2001). For this project, we selected measures related to social skills, including social abilities and communication.

The Psychology Experiment Building Language software (PEBL) was employed for the assessment of executive functions (Mueller and Piper 2014). The EF skills evaluated included updating (assessed with the n‐back test), planning (assessed with the Tower of London test), inhibitory control (assessed with the go‐no‐go test), and working memory (assessed using the digit span test). Perceptual processing was measured using the block design, matrix reasoning, and visual puzzles subtests of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition (WAIS‐IV) (Wechsler 2008). In particular, the block design test measures visual‐motor skills, part‐whole recognition skills; matrix reasoning measures nonverbal reasoning; and visual puzzles measure visual processing and fluid reasoning skills, among others. Verbal abilities were evaluated using the information, similarities, and vocabulary subtests from the WAIS‐VI. Information measures how much general knowledge has been acquired from the environment; the similarities subtest measures abstract thinking and reasoning; and the vocabulary subtest measures the understanding of words and reflects language development, expressive skills, and retrieval of information from long‐term memory, among other abilities. In addition, verbal fluency was evaluated using the corresponding subtest from the BANFE (Batería Neuropsicológica de Funciones Ejecutivas) (Flores Lázaro et al. 2008). The distribution of participants' scores for each cognitive test is presented in Figure S1.

In the behavioral task data analysis, a Shapiro–Wilk test demonstrated that the behavioral task outcomes were not normally distributed (p < 0.01). Levene's test demonstrated that the variances between the statement categories were unequal (p < 0.01). Consequently, non‐parametric statistics were employed. The percentages and standard deviation are presented for the classification accuracy, and the median and interquartile range (IQR) for the latency of classification. A comparison between the statement categories was conducted using a Friedman test for repeated measures and a Durbin‐Conover pairwise comparison analysis with Bonferroni correction. Statistical tests were conducted using R (R Core Team 2003).

sec.title: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging
sec.p: The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) session was conducted on a 3‐Tesla General Electric MR750 scanner with a 32‐channel head coil. The acquisition parameters were as follows: for T1w, repetition time (TR) = 0.008 s, echo time (TE) = 0.003 s, flip angle = 12°, and matrix size = 256 × 256; for the functional sequence, the TE = 0.04 s, TR = 2 s, flip angle = 90°, and matrix size = 64 × 64. The imaging data conversion from DICOM to NIFTI format was conducted using the dcm2niix v1.0.20190902 software (Li et al. 2016). The preprocessing of the MRI data was done using the fmriprep pipeline (Esteban et al. 2019). The contextual discrepancy task presentation was optimized for the MRI scanner session using OPTSEQ (Dale et al. 1999) and was implemented in an event‐related design. The task was divided into three runs, with each run lasting 10 min. The participants were instructed to infer the speaker's intention when they heard the statement and to use the information provided by the context to accomplish this task. Prior to the beginning of the scan, the participants were presented with a training task, the objective of which was to familiarize them with the task at hand. This entailed the classification of four stimuli, with one stimulus per category. The stimuli used in the training task differed from those used within the scanner. The task was presented using NordicNeuroLab goggles, which were sourced from Bergen, Norway, and a response device, the Cedrus Lumina, which was procured from California, USA. Both the goggles and the response device were MRI compatible.

A whole‐brain analysis was conducted using the FMRI Software Library (FSL; v. 6.0.5) for subsequent analysis (Jenkinson et al. 2012). A general linear model (GLM) was employed for the initial (run), second (participant), and third (group) level analyses using the FEAT tool (Woolrich et al. 2004). At the initial level of analysis, the BOLD signal was examined during the presentation of the event of interest, namely the statements. To analyze the events, a GLM was performed using 15 regressors, four for each statement category (i.e., irony, literal, unrelated, and white lies), one for the fixation cross, and 11 for physiological regressors. The physiological regressors included cerebrospinal fluid, white matter, the global signal, DVARS, framewise displacement, and six motion regressors (translation and rotation in the x, y, z directions and pitch, roll, and yaw angles, respectively). As fmriprep does not perform smoothing, a 6‐mm smoothing kernel was applied at this level, and the significance threshold was adjusted at the cluster level (z = 2.3 and p < 0.05). To analyze the differences between the statement categories, 11 contrasts were examined. Four contrasts were tested to compare each statement category with the fixation cross (e.g., irony > fixation), four to compare each statement category with the other three (e.g., irony > white lies + literal + no relation), and three to compare irony with other statement categories (e.g., irony > white lies). A fixed effects GLM was performed for the second‐level analysis, which was conducted at the subject level. A mixed‐effects GLM (i.e., Flame 1) was employed for the third‐level analysis (group level). For both analyses, the threshold parameters of the initial level of analysis were maintained with cluster correction (z = 2.3, p < 0.05). To account for multiple comparisons, results were corrected using a Bonferroni‐adjusted significance threshold (11 models/0.05 = 0.0045). The functional activation areas (i.e., labels) were identified using the corresponding MNI152 template coordinates. The labels were obtained using the MNI to Talairach tool with the Brodmann areas in the Bioimage Suite Web (Papademetris et al. 2006), which defined the Brodmann areas in MNI space (Lacadie et al. 2008).

sec.title: Regression Models
sec.p: To investigate the cognitive factors involved in detecting different statement categories (e.g., irony), stepwise regression models were employed, with statement category acting as a moderator. A moderator variable alters the relationship between a predictor (independent) and an outcome (dependent) (Tang et al. 2009). In this context, we aimed to determine whether the relationship between behavioral performance and neural responses during message processing in context (dependent variables) and cognitive domains (predictors) is moderated by the type of statement—irony, white lies, literal, and unrelated (moderator) or instead reflects a shared cognitive substrate.

To identify the variables contributing to the processing of statement categories, stepwise regression was performed. The process began with no predictors, followed by the sequential inclusion of the most significant predictors, and the removal of variables that did not enhance model fit. Prior to analysis, outliers were removed, and the data were normalized using the scale function in R. All analyses were conducted in R using the stepwiseAIC function from the MASS package (Venables and Ripley 2002).

The dependent variables were categorized into performance variables and neural outcomes. The performance variables included accuracy and latency of classification on the contextual discrepancy task. Neural variables included three Regions of Interest (ROIs) related to irony processing. Details regarding the selection and creation of these ROIs are provided below.

The independent variables, or predictors, were chosen based on the cognitive domains under evaluation: social cognition, EF, perceptual processing, and verbal abilities. For social cognition, total scores from the RMET, SST, IRI, SSS, and the AQ subscales (communication, social skills, and imagination) were included. For EF, the Go/No‐go, Tower of London, digit span, and n‐back tasks were included. For perceptual processing, the WAIS‐IV subtests block design, matrix reasoning, and visual puzzles were selected. Finally, for verbal abilities, the WAIS‐IV subtests information, similarities, and vocabulary were used, and the verbal fluency test from the BANFE was included. The statistical descriptive results from these measures are available in Table S1.

The dependent variables at the neural level were selected based on the results of a meta‐analysis (Reyes‐Aguilar et al. 2018), with BOLD signal percentage extracted from the ROIs using the feat_query tool on FSL for each subject and condition. To obtain the BOLD signal, contrasts comparing each statement category (ironic, white lies, literal, and unrelated) with the fixation cross (e.g., ironic statements > fixation) were selected. The ROIs chosen, based on a meta‐analysis of irony studies (24), included the dmPFC (x = 2, y = 54, z = 20), IFG (x = −50, y = 16, z = 4), pSTG (x = −60, y = −40, z = 12), and rmPFC (x = 2, y = 56, z = 16). Each ROI had a radius of 8 mm and was constructed using the fslmaths function (Woolrich et al. 2004). In total, 20 models were built, with 5 dependent variables and 4 cognitive domains as predictors. As an illustrative example, in this model the dependent variable (%BOLD IFG) was predicted by statement type—such as irony (I), unrelated (U), and white lies (WL)—as well as by a set of individual difference measures from the executive functions (EF). The results were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni correction, with the significance threshold set at 0.05. The adjusted significance level was set to 0.002 (0.05/20). Additionally, the relative importance of the overall models and each of the significant independent predictors was assessed using the relaimpo package (Groemping 2007) in R.

sec.title: Contextual Discrepancy Task
sec.p: The results revealed the lowest percentage of correct responses for ironic statements (71.43 ± 28.16), followed by white lies (78.57 ± 20.04), literal (85.71 ± 13.52), and the highest accuracy for unrelated statements (92.86 ± 14.64). Ironic statements had the longest latency of classification (Mdn = 1.91 s, IQR = 1.01), followed by literal (Mdn = 1.72, IQR = 0.87), white lies (Mdn = 1.49, IQR = 1.20), and unrelated statements (Mdn = 1.31, IQR = 0.84). The results demonstrated a statistically significant difference in the percentage of correct answers (χ 2 Friedman(3) = 45.68, p < 0.001) and latency of classification (χ 2 Friedman(3) = 31.81, p < 0.001). Significant differences were observed in the percentage of correct responses between the statement categories, specifically between irony and literal (p < 0.05), unrelated (p < 0.001), and white lies (p < 0.001). Additionally, significant differences were noted between the unrelated statements and literal (p < 0.001) and white lies (p < 0.001; see Figure 2A). The latency of classification exhibited notable differences between the ironic statements and the unrelated (p < 0.001) and white lies (p < 0.001), as well as between literal compared with unrelated (p < 0.001) and white lies (p < 0.001; see Figure 2B).

sec.title: The Contrast Between One Statement Category Versus the Others
sec.p: The contrast irony > literal + unrelated + white demonstrated notable differential activation in the precuneus, specifically in Brodmann's area (BA) 31 (see Figure 3A; Table 1). The contrast literal > irony + unrelated + white lies demonstrated significant differential activation in three clusters: the right premotor area + supplementary motor area (SMA; BA 6), the left primary motor area (PMA; BA 4), extending to the primary sensory area (BA 1), and the right putamen, extending to the caudate (see Figure 3B and Table 1). The contrast unrelated > irony + literal + white lies demonstrated significant differential activation in three clusters: the left premotor area + SMA (BA 6), extending to the ventral anterior cingulate gyrus (BA 24); the left superior parietal lobule, extending to the supramarginal gyrus; and the right primary motor, extending to the premotor + SMA (see Figure 3C and Table 1). The contrast white lies > irony + literal + unrelated did not yield statistically significant results.

sec.title: Comparing Irony With Other Statements
sec.p: The irony > literal contrast showed significant differential activation in three clusters: the precuneus (BA 7 and 31), the left angular gyrus (BA 39), extending into the middle temporal gyrus (BA 21), and the right IFG (BA 45 and BA 44), extending into the dLPFC (BA 9 and 46) (see Figure S2A and Table S1). The irony > unrelated contrast showed significant differential activation in two clusters: the right secondary visual (BA 18), extending into the primary visual (BA 17), and the precuneus (BA 31), extending to the ventral cingulate and secondary visual. The irony > white lies contrast showed significant differential activation in two clusters: the right supramarginal gyrus (SMG; BA 40), extending into the precuneus (BA 7), cingulate gyrus (BA 31), and IFG (BA 44). Additionally, significant differential activation was observed in the left primary sensory (BA 1) (see Figure S2A–C and Table S1).

sec.title: Regression Models
sec.p: As detailed in the methods, a stepwise regression model was used with the statement category as a moderator to assess which cognitive domains were related to the accuracy and latency of classification. We used the same approach to find the cognitive domains that significantly predicted the activation of regions related to irony, specifically the dmPFC, IFG, and pSTG in the left hemisphere. The coordinates of these regions were obtained from a meta‐analysis of pragmatic language (Reyes‐Aguilar et al. 2018). The categories of the predictors were social cognition, EF, verbal abilities, and perceptual processing, as previously described.

sec.title: Performance on the Contextual Discrepancy Task
sec.p: The EF model was significant in predicting accuracy in the processing of the statement categories (F[3, 133] = 9.96, p < 0.001, adjusted R 2 = 0.16), explaining 18.34% of the variance in accuracy classification. The go‐no‐go task was the largest positive predictor (β = 0.30, SE = 0.08, t = 3.54, 95% CI [0.13, 0.47], p < 0.001), accounting for 8.13% of the variance. This was followed by the ToL task (β = 0.28, SE = 0.09, t = 3.12, 95% CI [0.10, 0.46], p < 0.01), which explained 6.71% of the accuracy. In contrast, the n‐back task was a negative predictor of accuracy (β = −0.27, SE = 0.09, t = −3.15, 95% CI [−0.45, −0.10], p < 0.01), accounting for 3.50% of the variance. These predictors evaluate inhibitory control, planning, and working memory, respectively (see Figure S3A–C).

Similarly, the EF model predicted the latency of classification of the statement categories (F[3, 128] = 7.79, p < 0.001, adjusted R 2 = 0.13), explaining 18.34% of the variance. The go‐no‐go (β = −0.25, SE = 0.08, t = −2.95, 95% CI [−0.19, 0.11], p < 0.01) and the ToL tasks (β = −0.26, SE = 0.08, t = −3.01, 95% CI [0.10, 0.46], p < 0.01) were significant negative predictors, explaining 8.13% and 6.71% of the variance in classification time, respectively. The n‐back task contributed to the model's overall significance but was not an independent significant predictor (β = 0.15, SE = 0.08, t = 1.85, 95% CI [−0.45, −0.10], p = 0.06) (see Figure S4A,B).

Additionally, the perceptual processing model was significant in predicting classification time (F[3, 160] = 4.34, p < 0.05, adjusted R 2 = 0.06). The matrix reasoning subtest was the largest predictor (β = −0.20, SE = 0.07, t = −2.63, 95% CI [−0.36, −0.05], p < 0.01), followed by block design (β = 0.20, SE = 0.08, t = 2.5, 95% CI [0.04, 0.37], p < 0.05), which explained 3.36% and 2.58% of the variance, respectively. The visual puzzles subtest contributed to the overall model significance but was not an independent significant predictor (β = −0.14, SE = 0.08, t = −1.70, 95% CI [−0.29, 0.21], p = 0.09) (see Figure S4C,D).

sec.title: Neural Measures
sec.p: In the left IFG, the model that included social cognition was significant (F[4, 154] = 4.67, p < 0.05, adjusted‐R 2 = 0.08), explaining 10.83% of the variance of the differential activation. The AQ social skills were the largest predictor (β = −0.31, SE = 0.08, t = −3.67, CI [−0.48, −0.14], p < 0.001), followed by the empathy measures by IRI (β = 0.20, SE = 0.08, t = 2.53, CI [0.04, 0.37], p < 0.05); these predictors explained 6.74% and 2.23% of the variance in the IFG activation, respectively (Figure S5A,B).

In addition, the model that included perceptual processing was significant (F[3, 170] = 10.56, p < 0.001, adjusted‐R 2 = 0.14), explaining 15.71% of the variance in the differential activation of the left IFG. Among the predictors, matrix reasoning was the largest contributor (β = −0.17, SE = 0.07, t = −4.15, CI [−0.43, −0.13], p < 0.001), followed by the visual puzzles (β = 0.28, SE = 0.07, t = 3.89, CI [0.14, 0.43], p < 0.001) and block design subtests (β = −0.17, SE = 0.07, t = −2.20, CI [−0.32, −0.02], p < 0.05). These predictors accounted for 8.12%, 5.53%, and 2.05% of the variance in left IFG differential activation, respectively. It is worth noting that the type of statement (e.g., irony, white lies, unrelated, and literal) and the interaction between statement categories and cognitive predictors were not significant predictors of the differential activation in the IFG (Figure S6A–C). For other regions of interest (ROIs) and cognitive domains, no models were significant.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the cognitive domains and neural mechanisms involved in the processing of ironic statements in a Spanish‐speaker sample. Our findings revealed that ironic statements were particularly challenging to detect, as evidenced by the lowest accuracy and the highest classification latency among all statement categories. This difficulty reflects the inherent complexity of irony as a form of pragmatic language. Unlike literal or straightforward statements, irony requires the integration of multiple cognitive processes, including inferencing the speaker's intended meaning, detecting a contrast between literal content and contextual cues, and managing social and emotional subtleties (Pexman 2008; Valles‐Capetillo et al. 2022). These demands contribute to the view that irony is one of the most complex forms of communication (Sperber and Wilson 1981). In terms of neural activation, the precuneus, a region found to be primarily associated with processing ToM, was consistently engaged during the processing of ironic statements. The precuneus activation was found in all contrasts between ironic statements and other statement categories (literal and unrelated). Conversely, when literal or unrelated statements were compared with all other categories, they showed activation in motor‐related regions (e.g., BA 4 and 6), potentially reflecting preparatory or embodied processing. Furthermore, the analysis of white lies versus other categories did not reveal a distinct activation pattern, indicating that white lies might engage overlaying neural networks with other forms of communication or rely on more distributed processing. Regression analyses further indicated that detecting the four statement categories (i.e., ironic statements, white lies, unrelated statements, and literal statements) relied on overlapping cognitive domains, encompassing EF, perceptual processing, and social cognition. These results underscore the shared cognitive demands required for linguistic inferences across diverse contexts (Hauptman et al. 2023).

The whole‐brain analysis revealed significant differential activation in the left precuneus when irony was contrasted with all other statement categories and irony with each individual statement. The involvement of the precuneus during irony aligns with studies by Shibata et al. (2010) and Varga et al. (2013), highlighting the role of the precuneus in processing irony across different cultures, such as Japanese and Hungarian. Moreover, this area has also been implicated in other forms of pragmatic language, including speech acts (Licea‐Haquet et al. 2019; Shibata et al. 2011; van Ackeren et al. 2012) and metaphor processing (Desai et al. 2011; Schmidt and Seger 2009; Yang et al. 2009). Beyond its role in pragmatic processing, the precuneus has also been implicated in mental imagery and the construction of inferential meanings (Amodio and Frith 2006; Cavanna and Trimble 2006; Frith and Frith 2006; Gallagher et al. 2000; Mar et al. 2008; Schnell et al. 2016; Schurz et al. 2014). Thus, precuneus activation during processing irony suggests its central role in the inferential process required for interpreting ironic meaning (Licea‐Haquet et al. 2019). Notably, the precuneus did not exhibit differential activation for other statements, such as literal, white lies and unrelated, despite its previously reported involvement in processing other pragmatic forms like speech acts and metaphor. This absence may reflect the relatively lower inferential demands required by these conditions, in contrast to the more complex perspective‐taking and mentalizing processes typically elicited by irony.

Based on a previous meta‐analysis (Reyes‐Aguilar et al. 2018), we expected the processing of irony to involve significant activation in key regions, including the dmPFC (BA 9), IFG (BA 44), and STG (BA 22). Consistent with this hypothesis, we found differential activation in the right IFG in the contrasts between irony and literal, as well as irony and white lies. The IFG is classically associated with language processing (Friederici and Gierhan 2013), including the processing of unusual or incongruous semantic fields (Jung‐Beeman 2005; Obert et al. 2016), semantic violations, reanalysis of meanings (Bašnáková et al. 2014), integration of linguistic information into context (Shtyrov and Pulvermüller 2007), and selection of socially appropriate interpretations (Egorova et al. 2016). Supporting this finding, event‐related potential (ERP) studies have reported increased N400 amplitudes, associated with detecting anomalous linguistic information, particularly when evaluating irony based on prosody or context (Cornejol et al. 2007; Regel et al. 2010; Regel and Gunter 2017). These findings collectively underscore the IFG's critical role in resolving the semantic and social complexities inherent in processing irony.

As hypothesized, the contrast between ironic and literal statements also led to activation in the pSTG, an area commonly associated with social processes such as ToM (Amodio and Frith 2006; Gallagher et al. 2000; Mar et al. 2008), action observation (Yang et al. 2015), extracting social information (Egorova et al. 2016; Redcay 2008), and integrating paralinguistic cues with contextual information (Egorova et al. 2016). ERP studies investigating processing irony have consistently shown an increase in the P600, which is linked to the integration of information, a prerequisite for processing irony (Regel and Gunter 2017; Spotorno et al. 2013; Weissman and Tanner 2018). Similarly, eye‐tracking research using context to detect irony has reported increased regressions, which are thought to reflect the integration of key information needed to infer ironic meaning (Filik et al. 2017; Filik and Moxey 2010; Olkoniemi et al. 2019). Together, these findings underscore the importance of information integration in the processing of irony, highlighting the role of the pSTG in processing both social cues and contextual information.

In addition, the contrast between ironic and literal statements revealed differential activation in the right dlPFC, a region associated with goal‐oriented attention, task switching, planning, novelty seeking (Jones and Graff‐Radford 2021), problem‐solving, and working memory (Jones and Graff‐Radford 2021; Mansouri et al. 2007). This region likely plays a role in processing the ambiguity of the message within context and the nonliteral meaning, particularly when integrating cues to infer the intended linguistic meaning (Hertrich et al. 2021).

Another aim of this study was to explore the cognitive domains involved in processing irony through a comprehensive battery of tests evaluating social cognition, EF, perceptual processing, and verbal abilities—domains identified as essential for pragmatic language comprehension (Bosco et al. 2018; Hauptman et al. 2023; Howard et al. 2023; Martin and McDonald 2003; Pexman 2008). These cognitive factors were assessed in relation to performance on a contextual discrepancy task involving four statement categories: irony, white lies, unrelated statements, and literal statements. Regression analyses revealed that accuracy in processing irony, classification latency, and changes in the BOLD signal in the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) across the four statement types relied on overlapping cognitive domains of social cognition, EF, and perceptual processing. However, contrary to our expectations, the activation of the dmPFC and pSTG was not predicted by these cognitive domains. These findings suggest that regardless of the type of statement, understanding a statement within its contextual framework engages similar cognitive and neural mechanisms (Hauptman et al. 2023).

In the social cognition model, empathy and social skills, as measured by the IRI and the AQ social skills subscale, were significant individual predictors of changes in the % of BOLD signal of the IFG. These results are consistent with previous research linking the IFG to empathic responses (Li et al. 2020). The IFG has also been associated with the mirror neuron system, which plays a crucial role in understanding others' intentions, supporting imitation, and fostering empathy (Iacoboni and Dapretto 2006). These findings highlight the important role of social cognition—particularly empathy and social skills—in interpreting language within contextual frameworks.

EF, such as inhibitory control, planning, and working memory, was also a significant predictor of accuracy and latency classification. These functions were assessed using the Go/No‐Go, Tower of London, and Digit N‐Back tasks, respectively. The results align with Pexman's (2008) model and findings from contextual discrepancy tasks, which report that individuals with higher levels of EF skills demonstrate fewer social pragmatic difficulties (Howard et al. 2023; Olechowska et al. 2025). This underscores the crucial role of EF in language processing and pragmatic language.

One of our hypotheses suggested that a global perceptual processing style—central coherence, which focuses on broad patterns of information—would be associated with processing irony. Indeed, perceptual processing successfully predicted classification latency and changes in the BOLD signal in the left IFG, particularly through participants' ability to solve novel problems, perceive relationships, and complete visual analogies, as assessed with the matrix reasoning and visual puzzles subtests of the WAIS. This finding aligns with previous research that links perceptual processing with nonliteral language (Martin and McDonald 2003) and underscores the role of the left IFG in sentence‐context integration (Shtyrov and Pulvermüller 2007). Together, these results emphasize that perceptual processing plays a crucial role in detecting linguistic information during social interactions, further illustrating the interplay between perceptual and linguistic processing.

Unexpectedly, verbal abilities did not significantly predict performance on the contextual discrepancy task measures or changes in the BOLD signal in the selected regions of interest (ROIs). This may reflect a ceiling effect in neurotypical adults, where limited variability in verbal abilities within the sample could obscure potential relationships with the different statement categories (i.e., irony, white lies, unrelated, and literal).

In conclusion, the selection of a heterogeneous sample of participants enabled us to examine the effects of various cognitive domains involved in dealing with messages within a context, particularly ironic, white lies, unrelated, and literal statements. The results partially align with Pexman's (2008) constraint satisfaction model, which suggests that detecting the intended message—such as an ironic statement—relies on making inferences about the mental states of others (i.e., Theory of Mind, ToM) and verbal abilities (Pexman 2008). This was reflected in the activation of brain areas related to ToM, including the precuneus, and areas involved in language processing, such as the IFG and pSTG, as expected based on a previous meta‐analysis of pragmatic language (Reyes‐Aguilar et al. 2018). Furthermore, the regression models demonstrated that detecting a message within context, regardless of its intention (e.g., irony), requires the involvement of executive functions, perceptual processing, and social cognition.

This study introduces a task designed specifically for Spanish speakers, which can be used in fMRI experiments. This is particularly significant given that Spanish is spoken by nearly 500 million people—around 6.2% of the global population—making it the second most spoken language in terms of native speakers (Fernández Vítores 2023). A key advantage of this task is that the same statement is used for each interpretation—irony, white lies, literal, and unrelated—with the context being the determining factor in shaping the meaning. This is particularly significant because misinterpretations can easily occur if contextual cues are not properly recognized, or if the cognitive processes required to interpret the message are disrupted (Pexman 2008). While the statement categories share certain psycholinguistic properties, they also differ in important ways. For instance, both irony and white lies are context‐dependent and can be inappropriate in certain situations. However, these two conditions differ in their sincerity, with irony generally regarded as more sincere than white lies (Valles‐Capetillo et al. 2022). In this task, irony is used to joke about a situation, while white lies are employed to hide the truth and protect the listener from harm.

One limitation of the current study is the absence of a cognitive control domain—i.e., a domain not theoretically linked to irony processing. While our selection of social cognition, executive functions, verbal skills, and perceptual processing was guided by strong theoretical and empirical foundations from previous research (e.g., Pexman 2008; Martin and McDonald 2003), including a cognitive measure unrelated to pragmatic language could have helped us demonstrate the specificity of observed associations. However, the length of the neuropsychological battery, which required a minimum of 2 h and up to 4 h with participant‐requested breaks, limited the flexibility in additional tests. Future studies may benefit from incorporating control domains to further delineate the specificity of cognitive contributions to irony comprehension. Another limitation of this study is the selection of the ROIs for the regression models. We only selected areas directly related to processing irony. However, the regression models demonstrated that similar cognitive domains predict changes in the BOLD signal across the different statement categories. Therefore, exploring other areas related to pragmatic language in general would help clarify which cognitive domains are shared across different categories and which ones differ. Additionally, future studies would benefit from evaluating the effect of psycholinguistic properties during processing irony. For example, examining how statements are perceived in terms of their irony, sincerity, appropriateness, or relevance and their relation to changes in the BOLD signal could provide more insight. Another limitation is the inconsistency in findings across previous experiments, while some experiments have shown significant relationships between cognitive domains and pragmatics, in particular irony, others have not (Bosco et al. 2018; Cordonier et al. 2020; Song et al. 2024; Valles‐Capetillo et al. 2022). This discrepancy may be due to sample variability, an issue that warrants further exploration using analyses that are more sensitive to individual differences. Including participants with social communication difficulties, such as those with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), would increase sample diversity and enhance our understanding of the relationship between cognitive domains, brain changes, and language comprehension in social interactions, such as processing irony. Additionally, peak activation in the precuneus varied across Brodmann areas—with maxima localized to BA 31 for contrasts such as irony > all, irony > unrelated, and irony > white lies, and to BA 7 for irony > literal—all contrasts revealed clusters extending across both regions. This consistent overlap underscores the broader involvement of the precuneus in irony comprehension. Given the central role of the precuneus in integrating contextual, self‐referential, and social‐cognitive processes, these findings raise important questions about the functional specialization within this region. Future research should aim to disentangle the specific contributions of its subregions, particularly BA 7 and BA 31, in processing socially embedded meanings and integrating contextual cues during communication. Finally, our study relied on contextual discrepancies to detect different statement categories, but in natural social communication, other cues, such as facial expressions and prosody, are also present. Using alternative stimuli, such as videos, would allow for a more ecologically valid study of processing irony.
